comparator.name: Sustainable Bioscience (BSc)
comparator.academicYear: 2026-2027 (Education and Examination Regulations Bachelor Sustainable Bioscience 2026-2027, Articles 4.5-4.9 and Appendix I, adopted 1 September 2026; programme pages checked 2026-10-05)
comparator.sourceNotes: The programme pages (s1, s2, s3, s4) describe the English-taught, three-year, full-time BSc in words only and give no EC; the curriculum page (s3) lists the semester structure and links to a course repository that could not be read from this environment. The 180-EC reconstruction therefore uses the 2026-2027 Education and Examination Regulations (s0, Articles 4.5 to 4.9 and Appendix I). Year 1: eight 5-EC courses, four 2.5-EC skills courses and two 5-EC projects. Year 2: seven elective 5-EC courses plus the one mandatory 5-EC course that determines the concentration, four elective 2.5-EC skills courses and two mandatory 5-EC projects (Research Projects III and IV). Year 3: four 5-EC concentration courses, two 2.5-EC concentration skills courses, the 5-EC Grand Challenge and the 30-EC Bachelor Thesis Research. Totals are 60 EC per year and 180 EC overall. Year 2 is an elective framework of about 30 options (about six courses and three skills courses per period); one coherent selection linked to the Planetary Systems concentration is instantiated (Ecology, Global Dynamics, Climate Change and Resilience in Food Systems, Evolution, Applied Remote Sensing, Advanced Statistical Methods, Planetary Boundaries and Beyond the Sustainable Development Goals, with the skills Ecological Footprint, Engaging with Controversies in the Food System, Advanced Statistical Analysis using R and Big Data Analysis and Visualisation) and is flagged as an instantiation of restricted choice rather than a fixed requirement. In the Appendix I concentration table each period lists three items; the third is read as the 2.5-EC skills course, which the layout of the first-year skills columns supports but the text does not state. The programme is new for 2026-2027 and the curriculum page notes that course titles may change slightly. No course descriptions are published, so comparator components are characterised from their titles, the semester descriptions and the programme pages only.

routeSelection.basis: The generic bachelor has three formal concentrations (Planetary Systems, Agricultural Systems and Food Systems) of equal size (four 5-EC courses, two 2.5-EC skills courses) chosen in year 3. None is more representative of the programme's broad identity and none is less specialised; the programme pages and the Regulations (Appendix I) list Planetary Systems first, so it is used as the neutral tie-break. The choice is independent of UCR fit. It determines 25 EC of year 3 and, through the mandatory Planetary Boundaries course, one year-2 course.

core: Biological and laboratory foundations: biological systems, cell biology, biochemistry and biology laboratory skills (Biological Systems; Cell Biology; Biology Laboratory Skills)

Ecology, biodiversity, evolution and conservation: ecology from organisms to ecosystems, biodiversity through time, ecosystem services and conservation, with field-based landscape-ecology skills (Ecology; Evolution; Biodiversity Through Time; Biodiversity and Conservation; Skills for Landscape Ecology)

Earth systems, climate and planetary change: earth systems, planetary boundaries, climate change and resilience, global biogeochemical cycles, remote sensing and modelling of earth systems (Earth Systems; Planetary Boundaries; Global Biogeochemical Cycles; Applied Remote Sensing; Modelling Earth Systems)

Sustainable development and its governance: sustainable development, the Sustainable Development Goals and what lies beyond them, ecological footprint and global dynamics (Sustainable Development; Beyond the Sustainable Development Goals; Ecological Footprint; Global Dynamics)

Food, agriculture and nutrition foundations: food and nutrition, plant biology and sustainable food production, with biochemistry laboratory skills for food and nutrition (Food and Nutrition; Plant Biology)
Consumer behaviour and food choice: behavioural research into why people choose particular foods (Consumer Behaviour; Consumer and Sensory Analysis)
Mathematics, statistics, data analysis and programming for bioscience: mathematics for bioscience, statistical methods, statistics in R, advanced statistics and big-data analysis and visualisation
Research projects, field and laboratory skills and thesis: four year-1 and year-2 research projects, the year-3 grand challenge in sustainable system design and the 30-EC Bachelor Thesis Research
Ecosystem and human health: the link between biodiversity, ecosystems and human health, and public-health evidence (Planetary Health; Epidemiology of Food)
adjacent: Agricultural Systems concentration: plant biology, soil health, greenhouses, plant biotechnology and sustainable farming (Soil Science; Crop Physiology; Plant Breeding Skills)
Food Systems concentration: nutrition science, food technology and safety, and consumer behaviour (Food Functionality and Innovation; Clinical Nutrition; Food Safety)
questions: How can natural resources be used within planetary boundaries to meet society's needs?
How can what is known about plants, nature and the environment be used to grow food more sustainably, and how can people be given healthy, safe food without harming the planet?

trace: introduces the building blocks of life and how cells, molecules and systems interact to sustain living organisms; it directly implements the biological foundation that the first-year Biological Systems course provides, without that course's sustainability framing

teaches cell structure and physiology, mostly of eukaryotes, with the molecular mechanisms of life processes and applications that include agriculture and ecology; it directly implements the Cell Biology elective's subject but is not specific to plants

explores the chemistry of life, namely proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids, and metabolic pathways; it directly implements the biochemical part of the biological core, although it has no plant, food or nutrition focus

introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work, including bacteria, genetically modified organisms and data analysis, and gives practical laboratory training; it directly implements part of Biology Laboratory Skills but has no plant, food or ecological laboratory themes

teaches epidemiology and public health, how disease, risks and changes over time are studied and how evidence is evaluated, with environmental topics such as water and air quality; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the programme's link between ecosystem health and human health but does not address ecosystems or biodiversity directly

gives an overview of the living world through the tree of life, from bacteria and archaea to the diversity of eukaryotes and their ecological roles, with attention to planetary boundaries; it directly implements the biodiversity foundation of the ecology strand

studies the principles of ecology from individuals and populations to communities and ecosystems, environmental conditions and resources, and uses ecological modelling; it directly implements the Ecology course

examines the causes and effects of biodiversity loss, the mass extinctions and the actions that can reduce it; it directly implements the biodiversity-and-conservation content of the Planetary Systems concentration

studies the ecological processes of marine systems such as estuaries, rocky shores and coral reefs and the impact of human activities on them; it makes a specific complementary contribution by extending ecosystem ecology and biodiversity to marine habitats, which the programme does not name

treats sustainable farming: current practices and their environmental impact, alternatives such as organic farming and crop rotation, integrated pest management and precision agriculture; it directly implements the programme's sustainable-agriculture question, but it is UCR's only farming course and has no plant-biology, greenhouse or crop-breeding content
introduces earth science, including earth history, environmental geology and the management of water, soil and mineral resources; it directly implements the Earth Systems foundation

covers the drivers of anthropogenic climate change and its effects on the natural world, including feedback loops, ocean acidification and biomes, and its societal effects; it directly implements the climate content of Climate Change and Resilience in Food Systems and the Planetary Systems concentration, without a food-systems focus

explores the interactions of biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere and teaches system modelling with proxies and isotope tracers; it directly implements the Modelling Earth Systems skills course
teaches the analysis of satellite and drone imagery and geospatial data with GIS to study changes in the earth system; it directly implements Applied Remote Sensing

studies biogeochemical processes at the earth's surface, such as soil-mineral-water interactions and the leaching of nutrients, with geochemical modelling; it directly implements part of Global Biogeochemical Cycles at the scale of surface and soil processes rather than global cycles

uses the planetary-boundaries model to introduce sustainability and teaches the tools needed for later environment courses; it directly implements the planetary-boundaries framework of Planetary Boundaries and the sustainability concepts of Sustainable Development

examines how sustainability policy is made and enforced, which actors shape it and what makes policy effective; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the sustainable-development and Sustainable Development Goals strand but has no biological content

is a project course in which small teams carry out a sustainability research project for an external partner, with research design, field research and data analysis; it directly implements the educational function of the research projects and the sustainable-systems grand challenge, in sustainability rather than bioscience

integrates psychology into economics to explain how people decide, covering biases, heuristics and framing, and uses experiments; it makes a specific complementary contribution to consumer behaviour and food choice, but it is not specific to food

teaches research design, experimental design, sampling and descriptive and inferential statistics including analysis of variance; it directly implements the statistical-methods and research-design content of Statistical Methods and Data Analysis
teaches the basic mathematical techniques, such as differentiation, widely used in the sciences including biology; it directly implements the introductory Mathematics for Bioscience

covers probability theory, distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and statistical inference; it directly implements the mathematical foundation of the advanced statistics courses, although the UCR course is not specific to biological data

teaches data visualisation, cleaning and manipulation with hands-on science data sets, including spatial data; it directly implements Big Data Analysis and Visualisation and the data-science element of the programme

alternatives.label: Closest match to Sustainable Bioscience: Ecology, Earth Systems and Life Science with Data and Research Methods
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has five biology and biomedical-science courses (Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine, Molecular Cell Biology, Biochemistry, Life Science Laboratory, Epidemiology & Public Health), five ecology and biodiversity courses (Introduction to Biodiversity, Ecosystems Uncovered, Conservation Biology, Marine Biology, Sustainable Farming & Innovation), five earth-system and climate courses (Dynamic Earth, Climate Change, Earth System Science Tools, Earth Observation, Environmental Biogeochemistry), three sustainability courses (Sustainability Essentials I, Governance of Sustainability, Research in a Sustainable Delta), four methods and data courses (Mathematical Methods, Research Methods & Statistics, Probability & Statistics, Introduction to Data Science), Behavioral Economics and Personal & Professional Development. No single field dominates and UCR has no plant biology, nutrition or food-technology course, so the label names the ecology, earth-system and life-science content together with data and research methods and does not present the programme as a sustainable-bioscience degree.
alternatives.concept: Maastricht University's Sustainable Bioscience bachelor combines biological and earth systems, food and plant science, consumer behaviour, mathematics, statistics and data analysis with four research projects, a choice of 30 year-2 electives and a concentration (Planetary Systems, Agricultural Systems or Food Systems) before a 30-EC bachelor thesis. This alternative reproduces that core as closely as UCR's catalogue allows, following the generic programme's neutral Planetary Systems route: biological, cell and biochemical foundations with laboratory training; ecology, biodiversity and conservation science; earth-system, climate, biogeochemistry and remote-sensing science framed by planetary boundaries; the one sustainable-farming course UCR offers; sustainability governance and an applied research project; and mathematics, statistics and data-science methods, with consumer decision-making as the nearest counterpart of consumer behaviour.
progression: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine, Sustainability Essentials I, Introduction to Biodiversity and Personal & Professional Development open semester 1, and the courses that require the two gateways follow them: Molecular Cell Biology and Biochemistry (semesters 2 and 3) and Life Science Laboratory (semester 6) after Foundation of Life, Earth System Science Tools, Earth Observation and Environmental Biogeochemistry (semesters 4 and 5) after Sustainability Essentials I. Mathematical Methods (semester 2) precedes Probability & Statistics (semester 3), and Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) precedes Behavioral Economics (semester 6). Introductory ecology, conservation, earth-science and climate courses (semesters 2 to 4) precede the semester-5 Marine Biology and Environmental Biogeochemistry and the applied Research in a Sustainable Delta project, and Introduction to Data Science closes the programme with data skills after the earlier statistics.

selection.assessment: One UCR alternative is defensible. Alternative 1 owns ten generator-eligible rows that describe the programme's core and the Planetary Systems route (6357 sustainable bioscience, 6358 protecting biodiversity, 6359 using natural resources within planetary limits, 6362 climate change and food security, 6364 ecosystem and human health, 6365 ecology and environmental science, 6367 data science for environmental and biological research, 6368 food and the environment as connected systems, 6369 planetary systems and environmental change, 6372 climate, biodiversity and ecosystem resilience); the support-only rows 6377 to 6382 and the discovery rows strengthen its courses. Two further directions were tested. Sustainable agriculture, soils and plant biotechnology (rows 6360, 6363, 6366, 6370, 6373, 6374 and 6383, supported by 6378, 6380 and 6382) was rejected as not-substantively-distinct: UCR offers a single farming course (Sustainable Farming & Innovation) and no plant-biology, plant-breeding or greenhouse course, Alternative 1 already contains that course together with the soil and biogeochemistry, remote-sensing and molecular-biology courses, and the only agriculture-specific addition, Soils & Aquifers, would have to be combined with human-genetics, robotics and machine-learning courses whose link to crops is not evidenced, so the alternative would share about 19 of 24 courses without a genuinely different curriculum. Food systems, nutrition and food technology (rows 6361, 6371, 6375 and 6376, supported by 6377 and 6379) was rejected as not-feasible: UCR has no course in nutrition, food science, food technology or food safety and no consumer-food course, so the alternative would consist of Alternative 1's biochemistry, physiology and behavioural courses relabelled as food science. The search-only rows 6384 to 6397 generated no alternative and no row is inherited across split targets.

blocks: Biology, cell and molecular biology and laboratory skills

Both give the foundational biology of living systems; Foundation of Life covers the building blocks of life and how cells, molecules and systems interact, which is an important and identifiable part of the foundation that Biological Systems provides, whereas the Maastricht course is framed around biological systems relevant to sustainability and the programme publishes only its title and a semester description.

Both train biological laboratory skills; Life Science Laboratory teaches biochemical and molecular laboratory work, which is an important part of Biology Laboratory Skills, but its themes (blood, bacteria, genetically modified organisms) are biomedical rather than ecological or plant-based.

Both teach the principles of ecology; Ecosystems Uncovered covers ecology from individuals and populations to communities and ecosystems, which is the primary subject of Ecology, whereas the Maastricht elective is placed in a Planetary Systems course sequence and its description is not published.

Both address the diversity of life across time; Introduction to Biodiversity surveys the tree of life, including its palaeontological and molecular basis, which is an identifiable part of Biodiversity Through Time, but UCR does not teach the history of biodiversity in the same depth.

Both address the conservation of biodiversity; Conservation Biology treats the causes of biodiversity loss and actions to reduce it, which is the subject of Biodiversity and Conservation, although the Maastricht unit is a 2.5-EC skills course.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: no scheduled UCR course in this alternative teaches evolution; The Science of Evolution is not part of the programme.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: no scheduled UCR course treats ecosystem services directly; Ecosystems Uncovered is matched to Ecology.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the field-based landscape-ecology skills course has no UCR counterpart in this programme.
Earth systems, climate and planetary change

Both introduce the earth system; Dynamic Earth covers earth history, environmental geology and resource management, which is the primary subject of Earth Systems, although the Maastricht course is published only by title and a semester description.

Both address climate change and its effects; Climate Change covers its drivers and impacts on ecosystems, biomes and society, which is an important part of Climate Change and Resilience in Food Systems, but UCR does not treat food-system resilience or adaptation.

Both study the biogeochemical processes of the earth; Environmental Biogeochemistry covers surface and soil processes and nutrient leaching, which is an identifiable part of Global Biogeochemical Cycles, whereas the Maastricht unit treats the global cycles.

Both teach the modelling of the earth system; Earth System Science Tools teaches system modelling of interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere, which is the function of Modelling Earth Systems.
Both teach remote sensing; Earth Observation covers the analysis of satellite and drone data with GIS to study changes in the earth system, which is the primary method of Applied Remote Sensing.
Agriculture, food, nutrition and ecosystem health
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: UCR has no food or nutrition course.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: UCR has no plant-biology course.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: UCR has no food-and-nutrition laboratory skills course; Life Science Laboratory is matched to Biology Laboratory Skills.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: UCR has no course on controversies in the food system.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Epidemiology & Public Health addresses population health and evidence but not the health of ecosystems and the planet, so it is placed in a separate row as a complementary course.
Sustainability, governance, consumer behaviour and research projects

Both use the planetary-boundaries framework; Sustainability Essentials I introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries and the earth-system limits that define a safe operating space, which is the primary subject of Planetary Boundaries.

Both address the governance of the global sustainability agenda; Governance of Sustainability examines how sustainability policies are made, enforced and judged effective, which is an important part of Beyond the Sustainable Development Goals, but the Maastricht course is published only by title.

Both study how people choose; Behavioral Economics covers biases, heuristics and framing in decision-making, which is an important part of the behavioural research in Consumer Behaviour, but it is not specific to food or consumers.

Both are applied projects on sustainability challenges; Research in a Sustainable Delta has small teams carry out research for an external partner, which corresponds to the educational function of the sustainable-system-design grand challenge, in a sustainability rather than bioscience setting.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Sustainability Essentials I is matched to Planetary Boundaries and no other scheduled course teaches sustainable development in general.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: no scheduled UCR course corresponds to Global Dynamics.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the ecological-footprint skills course has no UCR counterpart.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the team project that applies the first semester's courses has no separate UCR counterpart.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the second-semester research project has no separate UCR counterpart.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the third research project has no separate UCR counterpart.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the fourth research project has no separate UCR counterpart.
Mathematics, statistics, data analysis and research

Both teach the mathematics used in the sciences; Mathematical Methods covers differentiation and other widely used techniques, which is an important part of Mathematics for Bioscience, but it is not tailored to biological applications.

Both teach research design and statistics; Research Methods & Statistics covers descriptive and inferential statistics, experimental design and analysis of variance, which is an important part of Statistical Methods and Data Analysis.

Both teach statistical inference; Probability & Statistics covers distributions, estimation and inference, which is an identifiable part of the foundation for Advanced Statistical Methods, whereas the Maastricht course is applied to bioscience data.

Both teach data analysis and visualisation; Introduction to Data Science covers data visualisation, cleaning and manipulation with science data sets, which is the primary subject of Big Data Analysis and Visualisation.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: no scheduled UCR course is a statistics-in-R skills course.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: no scheduled UCR course corresponds to advanced statistical analysis in R.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: UCR has no supervised thesis course; the optional independent research element is shown in this row.

notes.text: Both programmes include substantial study of biology, ecology, earth and climate systems, sustainability and the mathematics, statistics and data analysis used to study them. The Maastricht University Sustainable Bioscience bachelor additionally includes specialist work in plant biology, food and nutrition, food technology, laboratory skills for food and plant research, a concentration in Planetary, Agricultural or Food Systems and four research projects. UCR students can instead combine ecology, earth-system and life-science courses with data and research methods, but those specialist components are not offered at the same level of depth.

The Maastricht University Sustainable Bioscience bachelor organizes study around a fixed first year, an elective second year, a third-year concentration and a 30-EC thesis, with research projects at the end of every semester. At UCR, comparable subjects are distributed across courses in ecology, earth science, life science, sustainability, economics and data science. The UCR programme therefore covers related territory through a different curricular structure rather than reproducing the Maastricht programme course by course.
